blocks.text: Axolotl is a fine-tuning framework built around a config-file-driven workflow, where an entire training run, model, dataset, method, and hyperparameters, is specified in a single YAML file rather than assembled through Python code, an approach distinct from the code-first libraries covered earlier in this module.

This topic covers how the YAML configuration approach works, what it trades off against writing training code directly, and where Axolotl fits for teams that want reproducible, easily shared training setups.
1. Config-File-Driven Training
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472613325-60978304.png

Where Transformers, PEFT, and TRL, all covered in earlier topics, are used by writing Python code that calls their APIs, Axolotl instead asks you to describe an entire training run declaratively in a YAML file, and its own tooling reads that file and runs the corresponding training internally.
2. What Goes Into a Config File

blocks.alt: What Goes Into a Config File
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472613823-917442404.png

A typical Axolotl config specifies the base model to fine-tune, the dataset location and format, whether to use full fine-tuning or a parameter-efficient method like LoRA or QLoRA, both covered in earlier modules, and training hyperparameters, all in one readable file rather than scattered across code.

code.content:
base_model: meta-llama/Llama-3-8b
datasets:
  - path: my_dataset.jsonl
    type: alpaca
adapter: lora
lora_r: 16
lora_alpha: 32
learning_rate: 0.0002
num_epochs: 3

blocks.text: 3. Launching a Training Run
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472613825-184585069.png

Running a fine-tuning job with Axolotl is typically a single command line call pointing at the config file, with Accelerate, covered in an earlier topic, handling the underlying distributed training launch, no separate Python training script needs to be written for standard use cases.
4. Built on the Same Underlying Ecosystem

blocks.alt: Built on the Same Underlying Ecosystem
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472613826-136711348.png

Under the hood, Axolotl still uses Transformers, PEFT, and DeepSpeed, all covered in earlier topics of this module, its main contribution is the YAML configuration layer and workflow tooling on top, rather than a fundamentally different training implementation.

blocks.text: 5. Supporting Full Fine-Tuning and PEFT Methods

blocks.alt: Supporting Full Fine-Tuning and PEFT Methods
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472613826-73603883.png

A single config file setting switches between full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient methods like LoRA or QLoRA, both covered in earlier modules, making it straightforward to compare different fine-tuning strategies on the same base setup just by editing a few config lines.
6. Config Files vs Interactive Notebook Workflows

blocks.alt: Config Files vs Interactive Notebook Workflows
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472613827-197737695.png

The config file approach trades some of the flexibility of interactive, cell-by-cell notebook experimentation for reproducibility and easy sharing, a config file fully specifies a run in a way that is simple to version control, diff, and rerun exactly, a real advantage for teams running many similar experiments.

blocks.title: Reproducibility is the main design goal here
blocks.content: Because an entire training run configuration lives in one committed file, reproducing a specific past experiment, or handing a training setup to a teammate, is far more reliable than reconstructing the equivalent state from a notebook history.

blocks.text: 7. Handling Different Dataset Formats
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472613827-955358008.png

Axolotl supports several common dataset formatting conventions, instruction-style, chat-style, and others, out of the box through configuration, reducing the amount of custom data preprocessing code needed compared to writing formatting logic directly against Transformers datasets.
8. Axolotl vs Writing Code Directly

For a team running many broadly similar fine-tuning experiments that differ mostly in hyperparameters or dataset, Axolotl config-driven approach reduces repeated boilerplate significantly, for a team needing a highly custom training loop with unusual logic, writing directly against Transformers, PEFT, and TRL, all covered in earlier topics, offers more direct control.
9. When Axolotl Is a Good Fit

Axolotl tends to fit teams that value reproducibility, easy experiment comparison, and a lower barrier to running standard fine-tuning recipes, without needing every team member to be comfortable writing training code directly against the lower level libraries.
Worked Example

A team wants to run a systematic sweep comparing LoRA rank values, 8, 16, and 32, on the same base model and dataset. With Axolotl, they create three nearly identical YAML config files differing only in the lora_r value, and launch each as a separate, easily reproducible run.

Because each run configuration lives in a committed file, revisiting exactly what settings produced the best result later, or handing the winning config to a teammate to reproduce, requires no extra documentation beyond the file itself.
Common Mistakes

items: Choosing Axolotl for a highly custom training loop that its configuration options cannot actually express
Not version controlling config files, losing the reproducibility advantage the approach is meant to provide
Assuming Axolotl implements its own separate training logic rather than building on Transformers, PEFT, and DeepSpeed
Mismatching the dataset type setting in the config against the actual data format, producing malformed training examples

blocks.text: Practice

Sketch a YAML config for fine-tuning a model on a task you are familiar with, specifying base_model, a dataset entry, and an adapter method choice, then compare how many lines of Python code the equivalent setup would take using the direct Transformers and PEFT approach covered in earlier topics.
Key Takeaway

Axolotl replaces hand-written training code with a declarative YAML configuration file, built on top of the same Transformers, PEFT, and DeepSpeed foundations covered earlier in this module, trading some flexibility for reproducibility and a lower barrier to running standard fine-tuning recipes across many experiments.
